name: First-wave feminism
summary: First-wave feminism, from Wollstonecraft's 1792 Vindication through the Seneca Falls convention (1848), Mill's Subjection of Women and the suffrage campaigns to about 1920, claimed for women the legal and political standing of men: the vote, the control of their own property and earnings, equal marriage and guardianship law, education and the professions, and one moral standard. It argued from natural rights and the consent of the governed, and from the movement's own texts it said little on economics, foreign policy or most other political questions; strands differed on divorce, religion, the nature of women, and on whether to use militancy.
scope: The Anglo-American women's-rights and suffrage movement, 1792 to about 1920, taken from its own texts: the Seneca Falls Declaration and resolutions, the convention resolutions in the History of Woman Suffrage, Stanton, Anthony, Mill and Harriet Taylor Mill, Wollstonecraft, Willard's WCTU, Fawcett's constitutional suffragists and the Pankhursts' WSPU. It excludes second-wave, radical, socialist and intersectional feminisms and anything taken from liberalism, abolitionism or temperance as such; a position counts only where the movement's own sources state it.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments lists the denial of 'the elective franchise' as the first wrong and the Seneca Falls resolutions make securing it a duty; Mill's Subjection argues that women should vote under whatever conditions men do, and the movement's later platforms demand a sixteenth amendment.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Declaration of Sentiments states that governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed'; Anthony argued in 1873 that for women the government has no such just powers, and the 1876 convention reaffirmed the principle.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: The Seneca Falls resolutions state that no human law is valid if contrary to the law of nature and that laws placing woman in a position inferior to man's have 'no force or authority'; Anthony called every sex discrimination in state law 'null and void'.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The Declaration charges that 'the history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman', aimed at an 'absolute tyranny', and Mill calls the legal subordination of one sex to the other wrong in itself; the 1870s platforms call it an 'aristocracy of sex'.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Declaration protests that man 'usurped the prerogative of Jehovah himself' by assigning woman a sphere of action, and the Seneca Falls resolutions call laws keeping woman in a position inferior to man's void; Mill demands equality with no privilege or disability on either side.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: The Declaration objects that a wife promises obedience to a husband who becomes 'her master', and Mill argues the legal rule of obedience in marriage should give way to a principle of perfect equality; the 1850s resolutions say the marriage law 'may give to him in marriage a slave, or a tyrant, but never a wife'.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The Declaration charges that the husband 'has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns', and Mill shows that whatever a wife inherits or earns becomes her husband's and argues against it; the 1850s conventions demanded 'equal property rights' for married women.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Stanton and Blackwell argued at the 1860 national convention that divorce reform belonged on the platform, while Wendell Phillips objected to the resolutions as outside a woman's-rights convention, and an 1872 convention resolved that suffrage means 'greater permanency in marriage'; the movement took no common line.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: The Declaration complains that divorce law is framed regardless of women's happiness, and Stanton's divorce resolutions were pressed at the 1860 convention, but Phillips and others objected that divorce was not a woman's-rights question and Mill declined to discuss divorce; no common position on who may initiate it.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The Seneca Falls resolutions rest equality on 'the identity of the race in capabilities and responsibilities', but an 1872 suffrage-convention platform says women 'have peculiar feminine characteristics' in which they differ from men, and Willard's WCTU argued that women would bring 'a set of motives altogether new' to the ballot; strands split.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Stanton wrote that she found no explanation for the degraded status of women 'under all religions' and published the Woman's Bible, while suffrage and temperance conventions passed resolutions against it and Willard declined to take part; adherents split.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Stanton's Woman's Bible examined what the scriptures say of women and held the texts to no special authority, but suffrage and temperance conventions disapproved of it by resolution and Willard and others withdrew from the revising committee; strands split.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The Declaration says 'all men and women are created equal' and the 1860s Equal Rights Association resolutions demanded rights for women and colored people alike, but in 1869 Stanton and others opposed manhood suffrage with arguments ranking educated women above black men, and the movement split over the Fifteenth Amendment; the record is mixed.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Scholars read Wollstonecraft's view of freedom as independence from the arbitrary power of others, and Mill describes the wife as a bondservant under a master with legal power over her person and property; the Declaration likewise protests a husband's legal power over his wife's liberty.

self-ownership.rationale: The 1850s resolutions condemn marriage law that denies a wife 'the product of her own industry' and 'the custody of her own person', and Stanton grounds women's claims on a 'birthright to self-sovereignty'; the sources do not use the libertarian term.

political-violence-never.rationale: The Pankhursts' WSPU defended broken windows and destruction of property as 'the argument of the broken window pane', while Fawcett wrote that probably the majority of suffragists opposed physical violence as a means of political justice; the movement divided.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Declaration states a duty to throw off a despotic government, but the movement worked by petition and organisation, and Willard described the WCTU's path to the ballot as 'evolution rather than revolution' while the WSPU defended militancy; no common position.

gradual-change.rationale: An 1851 Indiana convention resolved that time-honored laws and customs infringing woman's equal rights 'should be immediately abolished' and the Declaration demands 'immediate admission' to rights, while Willard described the WCTU's route to the ballot as growth 'rather than by a forcing process'; strands split.

property-franchise.rationale: An 1853 convention urged women to petition legislatures for 'universal suffrage', and the 1851 Indiana convention based citizenship on 'capacity and morality' rather than property; the British strand asked only for the vote on the same terms as men.

missingStatements.text: Women should receive equal pay for equal work.
missingStatements.rationale: The 1851 Indiana convention resolved that 'woman should receive for equal labor, equal pay with man' and later conventions demanded equal pay for equal work.
missingStatements.declined: Accepted almost everywhere today, so not contested.

missingStatements.text: Women should be admitted to universities and the professions on the same terms as men.
missingStatements.rationale: The Declaration protests that all colleges were closed to women and that she is 'not known' as a teacher of theology, medicine or law; Mill argues women should be admissible to all occupations.
missingStatements.declined: Accepted almost everywhere today, so not contested.

missingStatements.text: A mother should have the same legal rights over her children as the father.
missingStatements.rationale: The Declaration protests divorce and guardianship law that gives all power to the man, Mill objects that children are by law the father's alone, and an 1850s resolution objects that the law denies the wife 'her right to her children'.

missingStatements.text: Men and women should be held to the same standard of sexual conduct.
missingStatements.rationale: A Seneca Falls resolution says the same virtue and delicacy required of woman should be required of man and the same transgressions visited with equal severity on both; the Declaration condemns a 'different code of morals for men and women'.

notes: Searched theme by theme in full texts: economy (resolutions on pay, property, labour, taxation: only the equal-pay and property positions are stated), government (franchise, consent, taxation, universal against educated suffrage), world (peace and war resolutions give no stated position beyond conventions treating them as aids to suffrage), liberty, society, culture, means, and ecology/technology/globalism (nothing). Abortion, sex work, same-sex marriage, immigration, alcohol prohibition as a general drugs policy and economic systems are not stated by the movement's own sources and are null; temperance, Fifteenth Amendment racial arguments and the Woman's Bible divided it.
